text: The man did not know the rest of my faults, for he would not have mentioned these only.
author: Epictetus
notes: Trimmed: the sentence begins with advice on what to reply when told someone speaks ill of you.

text: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals.
author: Epictetus
notes: The real wording behind the modern 'be content to be thought foolish and stupid'.

text: I must die. Must I then die lamenting?
author: Epictetus

text: Nothing great, said Epictetus, is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is.
author: Epictetus
notes: 'said Epictetus' is Arrian's narration, kept to avoid changing the wording.

text: Asses would rather have straw than gold.
author: Heraclitus

text: Dogs bark at every one they do not know.
author: Heraclitus
Heraclitus
notes: Burnet/Bywater numbering; DK 119. The real wording behind 'Character is destiny'.

text: He knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
author: Socrates
notes: Clause from mid-sentence; only change is capitalising 'He'. The real text behind 'I know that I know nothing'.

text: Alexander came and stood over him and said, "Ask of me any boon you like." To which he replied, "Stand out of my light."
author: Diogenes
notes: Opening clause 'When he was sunning himself in the Craneum,' cut. The popular 'out of my sun' wording is not Hicks.

text: To the question what wine he found pleasant to drink, he replied, "That for which other people pay."
author: Diogenes

text: "Have I bored you to death with my chatter?" "No, indeed; for I was not attending to you."
author: Aristotle
notes: Lead-in 'To the chatterbox who poured out a flood of talk upon him and then inquired,' and 'he replied,' cut; quoted words unchanged. An anecdote attributed to him, not from his own writings.

text: Being asked what is difficult, he replied, "To know oneself." "What is easy?" "To give advice to another."
author: Thales
notes: Excerpt from a longer run of questions and answers.

text: Do not announce your plans beforehand; for, if they fail, you will be laughed at.
author: Pittacus
notes: Whole sentence, unchanged. One of the Seven Sages' maxims.

text: He said he wondered why in Greece experts contend in the games and non-experts award the prizes.
author: Anacharsis

text: Send me a little pot of cheese, that, when I like, I may fare sumptuously.
author: Epicurus
notes: Unchanged. From Epicurus's own letters, quoted by Diogenes Laertius.

text: The gods have not revealed all things to men from the beginning, but by seeking they find in time what is better.
author: Xenophanes
notes: Whole fragment, unchanged. Burnet numbering matches DK 18.

text: The beginning is the most important part of any work.
author: Plato
notes: Socrates speaking. 'You know also that' cut and 'The' capitalised; ', especially in the case of a young and tender thing' onward cut.
